section.title: The Holiness of Offerings
section.sectionRationale: This continues the priestly holiness laws of chapter 21, now focused on how priests must handle the sacred offerings, who within priestly households may eat them, and the standard every sacrificial animal must meet, all guarding God's holy name from being profaned.
section.thesis: God requires that priests approach the sacred offerings only in a state of cleanness, that only the priestly household may eat them, and that every animal offered to Him be without blemish, because His holy name must not be profaned by careless handling of what is holy.
section.frameNote: Three movements: priests must be clean to eat the sacred offerings, and only priestly household members may eat them; every offering brought to the LORD, whether to fulfill a vow or as a freewill offering, must be without blemish or defect; and the closing call not to profane God's holy name, since He is the LORD who sanctifies and redeemed Israel from Egypt.

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses,
“Tell Aaron and his sons to treat with respect the {{qodashim|sacred offerings}} that the Israelites have consecrated to Me, so that they do not profane My holy name. I am the LORD.

Tell them that for the generations to come, if any of their descendants in a state of uncleanness approaches the sacred offerings that the Israelites consecrate to the LORD, that person must be cut off from My presence. I am the LORD.

If a descendant of Aaron has a skin disease or a discharge, he may not eat the sacred offerings until he is clean. Whoever touches anything defiled by a corpse or by a man who has an emission of semen,
or whoever touches a crawling creature or a person that makes him unclean, whatever the uncleanness may be,
the man who touches any of these will remain unclean until evening. He must not eat from the sacred offerings unless he has bathed himself with water.
When the sun has set, he will become clean, and then he may eat from the sacred offerings, for they are his food.
He must not eat anything found dead or torn by wild animals, which would make him unclean. I am the LORD.
The priests must keep My charge, lest they bear the guilt and die because they {{chalal|profane}} it. I am the LORD who sanctifies them.
No one outside a priest’s family may eat the sacred offering, nor may the guest of a priest or his hired hand eat it.
But if a priest buys a slave with his own money, or if a slave is born in his household, that slave may eat his food.
If the priest’s daughter is married to a man other than a priest, she is not to eat of the sacred contributions.
But if a priest’s daughter with no children becomes widowed or divorced and returns to her father’s house, she may share her father’s food as in her youth. But no outsider may share it.
If anyone eats a sacred offering in error, he must add a fifth to its value and give the sacred offering to the priest.
The priests must not profane the sacred offerings that the Israelites present to the LORD
by allowing the people to eat the sacred offerings and thus to bear the punishment for guilt. For I am the LORD who sanctifies them.”

media.alt: A spotless lamb presented at an altar
media.caption: Every animal offered to the LORD must be without blemish or defect.

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses,

“Speak to Aaron and his sons and all the Israelites and tell them, ‘Any man of the house of Israel or any foreign resident who presents a gift for a burnt offering to the LORD, whether to fulfill a vow or as a freewill offering,
must offer an {{tamim|unblemished}} male from the cattle, sheep, or goats in order for it to be accepted on your behalf.
You must not present anything with a defect, because it will not be {{ratzon|accepted}} on your behalf.
When a man presents a peace offering to the LORD from the herd or flock to fulfill a vow or as a freewill offering, it must be without blemish or defect to be acceptable.

You are not to present to the LORD any animal that is blind, injured, or maimed, or anything with a running sore, a festering rash, or a scab; you must not put any of these on the altar as an offering made by fire to the LORD.
You may present as a freewill offering an ox or sheep that has a deformed or stunted limb, but it is not acceptable in fulfillment of a vow.
You are not to present to the LORD an animal whose testicles are bruised, crushed, torn, or cut; you are not to sacrifice them in your land.
Neither you nor a foreigner shall present food to your God from any such animal. They will not be accepted on your behalf, because they are deformed and flawed.’”

units.label: Practical timing, and God's holy name

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses,
“When an ox, a sheep, or a goat is born, it must remain with its mother for seven days. From the eighth day on, it will be acceptable as an offering made by fire to the LORD.
But you must not slaughter an ox or a sheep on the same day as its young.
When you sacrifice a thank offering to the LORD, offer it so that it may be acceptable on your behalf.
It must be eaten that same day. Do not leave any of it until morning. I am the LORD.
You are to keep My commandments and practice them. I am the LORD.
You must not profane My holy name. I must be acknowledged as holy among the Israelites. I am the LORD who sanctifies you,
who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God. I am the LORD.”

qodashim.gloss: Sacred or holy offerings, the food consecrated to God and then given to the priesthood for their sustenance. Treating these carelessly, whether through uncleanness or wrongful sharing, was treated as profaning God's own name.

chalal.gloss: To profane, defile, or treat as common what is holy. Applied throughout this chapter to careless handling of the sacred offerings and, at its close, to God's own holy name, tying priestly conduct directly to God's reputation among the people.

tamim.gloss: Without blemish, whole, or perfect. The required standard for every sacrificial animal, later applied metaphorically to a person's integrity, and ultimately fulfilled in the New Testament's description of Christ as a lamb without blemish or defect.

ratzon.gloss: Acceptance, favor, or that which is pleasing. Repeated throughout this chapter to describe what makes an offering acceptable before God, showing that not every gift, however sincerely offered, automatically pleases Him; the offering itself must meet His standard.

basic.context: This chapter first regulates how priests must be ceremonially clean to eat the sacred offerings, and who within a priestly household may share that food, then turns to require that every animal offered to the LORD, whether for a vow or a freewill offering, be without blemish or defect.
basic.hermeneutics: This is ceremonial and cultic law for Israel's priesthood and sacrificial system, not a dietary or ritual rule for Christians today. Its enduring principle, that God deserves the best, not the leftover or the flawed, and that careless worship dishonors His name, still teaches the church and is fulfilled in Christ's own perfect self-offering.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter turns on qodashim, sacred offerings, which must not be chalal, profaned, by careless priestly conduct, and on tamim, without blemish, the required standard every sacrifice must meet in order to secure ratzon, acceptance, before God.
basic.typology: The requirement that every offering be without blemish anticipates Christ, described as a lamb without blemish or defect, whose precious blood, not silver or gold, secures His people's redemption, 1 Peter 1:18-19.
basic.christ: 1 Peter 1:18-19 says believers were redeemed with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or defect, exactly the standard this chapter sets for every sacrificial animal. Where Israel had to search their flocks for a flawless animal, God provided, in His own Son, the one perfect and sufficient offering His own law required.
basic.god: God's holiness will not be honored by careless or blemished worship; who may approach His holy things and what may be offered to Him both matter, because His own name and reputation are bound up with how He is worshiped. Yet cleanness is always available through washing and time, and the standard He sets, He Himself ultimately meets in Christ.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Peter 1:18-19 describes believers redeemed by the precious blood of a lamb without blemish. Malachi 1:8 rebukes Israel for later offering God blind, lame, or sick animals, violating this very chapter. Hebrews 10:22 invites believers to draw near with hearts sprinkled clean and bodies washed with pure water. 1 Corinthians 11:27-29 calls believers to examine themselves before approaching the Lord's table.
basic.oneStory: God's insistence on cleanness among His priests and flawlessness in every offering teaches that true worship costs something real and cannot be careless. That standard, impossible for sinful people to meet in themselves, is fulfilled completely when Christ, the spotless Lamb, offers Himself once for all, so that His people can now approach God with clean hearts through Him.

context.literary:
Chapter 22 completes a two chapter unit on priestly holiness. Chapter 21 was about the priest's person: whom he mourns, whom he marries, what his body is like. Chapter 22 is about what passes through his hands: the holy food, who may share it, and what may be laid on the altar. The two chapters move from the man to the meal to the offering, drawing steadily closer to the altar itself.

The chapter has three speeches, each opened with 'Then the LORD said to Moses,' verses 1, 17 and 26. The first, verses 2 to 16, is addressed to Aaron and his sons only. The second, verses 18 to 25, widens to 'Aaron and his sons and all the Israelites,' and even includes the foreign resident, because every worshipper who brings an animal must know the standard. The third, verses 27 to 33, gathers miscellaneous rules on timing and closes the whole holiness section with a solemn summary.

The repetition is deliberate. 'I am the LORD' sounds five times in the first speech alone, verses 2, 3, 8, 9 and 16, and the chapter closes with it twice more in verses 31 to 33. The refrain 'the LORD who sanctifies' appears at verses 9, 16 and 32, echoing chapter 21. The key word of the second speech is 'accepted' or 'acceptable,' which appears in verses 19, 20, 21, 23, 25, 27 and 29. Its key contrast is between tamim, 'unblemished,' and mum, 'defect,' the same word that barred the priest from the altar in 21:17-23. Priest and animal alike must be whole.

The final paragraph, verses 31 to 33, is the capstone of the holiness laws that began in chapter 17. It gathers the refrains: keep My commandments, do not profane My holy name, I must be acknowledged as holy, I am the LORD who sanctifies you, who brought you out of Egypt. The next chapter turns to sacred time, the appointed feasts.
context.historical:
The priests lived from the altar. Numbers 18:8 says God gave 'all the sacred offerings of the Israelites' to Aaron and his sons as their portion, and Numbers 18:11 extends some of that food to 'every ceremonially clean person in your household.' This made the question of who could eat a practical one in every priestly home. A guest or hired worker, verse 10, stood outside the household. A slave bought with the priest's money or born in his house, verse 11, belonged to it. The same distinction governs the Passover in Exodus 12:43-45, where a purchased slave may eat after circumcision but 'a temporary resident or hired hand shall not.'

The priest's daughter illustrates how belonging worked in ancient households. Married outside the priesthood, she ate at her husband's table, verse 12. Widowed or divorced without children and returned to her father's house, she ate there again 'as in her youth,' verse 13. The law protected her from falling between two households.

The animals listed, cattle, sheep and goats, were the wealth of a pastoral people. To give an unblemished male was to give from the best breeding stock. That cost is exactly what later generations tried to avoid. Malachi's hearers brought 'blind animals,' 'the lame and sick ones,' Malachi 1:8, and he challenged them, 'Try offering them to your governor!' He also named the fraud: 'cursed is the deceiver who has an acceptable male in his flock and vows to give it, but sacrifices a defective animal,' Malachi 1:14.

The rule of verse 27, that a newborn must stay with its mother seven days, repeats Exodus 22:30. The rule of verse 28 against slaughtering a mother and its young on the same day belongs with Deuteronomy 22:6-7, the law of the bird's nest. The thank offering eaten the same day, verses 29 and 30, repeats Leviticus 7:15.
context.canonical:
The chapter's standard for offerings is the measuring rod the prophets used. Malachi 1:6-14 is almost a commentary on Leviticus 22 turned into an indictment: blind, lame, sick and stolen animals, priests who 'despise My name,' and the question 'Should I accept these from your hands?' Malachi 1:13. Against that failure God announces that 'in every place, incense and pure offerings will be presented in My name,' Malachi 1:11, among the nations. David had already stated the heart of the chapter: 'I will not offer to the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing,' 2 Samuel 24:24.

The prophets also insist that an unblemished animal is not enough. Psalm 51:16-17 says 'the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit,' and Micah 6:6-8 asks whether thousands of rams could please the LORD, answering with justice, mercy and humility. The outward wholeness of the offering was meant to be matched by the worshipper's heart.

The New Testament takes up the chapter's key terms. Christ 'offered Himself unblemished to God,' Hebrews 9:14, and believers are redeemed by 'a lamb without blemish or spot,' 1 Peter 1:19. Paul describes his ministry as 'priestly service' aimed at making 'the Gentiles... an offering acceptable to God,' Romans 15:16, and urges believers to present their bodies as 'living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God,' Romans 12:1. Hebrews 13:15-16 names praise and generosity as the sacrifices 'God is pleased' with. The chapter's closing prayer, that God's name be acknowledged as holy, becomes the first petition Jesus taught: 'hallowed be Your name,' Matthew 6:9.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to understand that God's name is at stake in ordinary handling of holy things. The chapter opens with the warning 'so that they do not profane My holy name,' verse 2, and closes with 'You must not profane My holy name,' verse 32. Everything in between, a priest eating after washing, a guest turned away from the table, a flawed ox refused at the altar, is framed as an act that either honours or cheapens the name of the God who redeemed Israel.

He also meant to protect the people. Verse 16 warns priests against 'allowing the people to eat the sacred offerings and thus to bear the punishment for guilt.' A careless priest would not only sin himself; he would drag others into guilt. Leadership in worship carries responsibility for those who follow.

The standard for animals taught the worshipper what acceptance meant. An offering was 'accepted on your behalf,' verses 19 to 21, not because the worshipper felt sincere, but because the gift met God's standard. That was a lesson in grace as much as demand. The worshipper did not earn acceptance by his own merit; he brought a substitute that met the requirement.

Finally, Moses tied it all to the exodus. The last words are 'who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God,' verse 33. Israel's care over holy things was a response to rescue. The God who had given His people freedom deserved their best, and He had first given them His.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The detailed rules of this chapter, which household members may eat, how long a priest waits after touching a corpse, which animals are acceptable, were prescribed for Israel's priesthood and altar. They are not binding on Christians, whose sacrifice has been offered once for all, Hebrews 10:10, and who have no altar of animal offerings. Even the food law of verse 8, which forbids the priest to eat what died naturally, is overtaken by the gospel's declaration that God has made foods clean, Mark 7:19.

What carries forward is the teaching the rules embodied. God is to be given what costs something, not leftovers. Worship is not safe when handled carelessly, which is why Paul warns against eating the Lord's Supper 'in an unworthy manner,' 1 Corinthians 11:27, and calls for self-examination first. Leaders are accountable for leading others into guilt. And acceptance before God rests on an offering that meets His standard, which the church finds in Christ alone, while its own sacrifices of praise and good works are 'acceptable to God through Jesus Christ,' 1 Peter 2:5.

debates.question: Is God's demand for an unblemished sacrifice merely about ritual perfectionism?

views.label: Teaching about the cost proper worship requires
views.case: Offering only unblemished, valuable animals meant worship cost something real, guarding against the temptation to give God what one would not want oneself. Malachi 1:8 makes the point with the governor comparison, and 2 Samuel 24:24 states it as a principle.

views.label: Foreshadowing the necessity of a truly sinless substitute
views.case: Others emphasise the forward looking function of the standard. The animal's physical wholeness pictures a moral wholeness no animal could have. Only a substitute wholly free of the real defect, sin, could fulfil what the law pointed toward, which Hebrews 9:14 and 10:4 draw out.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree this is not empty ritualism. The standard teaches the costliness of proper worship and anticipates the sinless substitute these animals could only picture. The first explains why a worshipper should bring his best; the second explains why even his best was never enough.

debates.question: Why are the young not to be slaughtered on the same day as their mother, verses 27-28?

views.label: Compassion for animals
views.case: Many read these laws, along with Exodus 22:30 and the bird's nest law of Deuteronomy 22:6-7, as teaching tenderness toward creatures. Proverbs 12:10 says 'A righteous man regards the life of his animal.' Even in sacrifice, Israel was to show restraint.

views.label: A boundary between life and death
views.case: Others see the concern as symbolic: the bond between a mother and her young represents the flow of life, and killing both together confuses what should be kept distinct. On this view the law belongs with the chapter's larger interest in separating what is holy and living from what is common and dead.

debates.bearing: The two readings need not compete. The law expresses reverence for the life God gives, which includes care for His creatures and respect for the order of life. It is a small window into a God who, in Jesus' words, does not forget a single sparrow, Luke 12:6.

debates.question: Why may a deformed animal be a freewill offering but not a vow offering, verse 23?

views.label: A vow is a debt; a freewill offering is a gift
views.case: A vow bound the worshipper to pay what he promised, and Malachi 1:14 condemns the one who vows an acceptable male and then substitutes a defective one. A freewill offering was spontaneous and so allowed some latitude. The distinction guards the integrity of promises.

views.label: Different kinds of offering carry different weight
views.case: Others note that the concession applies only to the peace offering context of verses 21 to 23, a meal shared by the worshipper, not to the burnt offering wholly given to God. The lesser flaw is tolerated where the offering is partly for the worshipper's own table.

debates.bearing: The text itself stresses the vow, so the first reading is on firmer ground. A promise made to God must be kept in full. Ecclesiastes 5:4-5 gives the same warning: it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter opens with an unexpected verb. 'Treat with respect,' verse 2, translates the passive stem of nazar, to separate or keep apart. Literally the priests are to 'separate themselves from' the holy things when unclean. The same root gives nezer, the high priest's consecration in 21:12, and nazir, the Nazirite. Respect for holy things is expressed as distance at the right time.

The holy offerings are qodashim, a plural of qodesh, holiness. Leviticus distinguishes 'the holy food' from 'the most holy food,' qodesh qodashim, in 21:22. Here the concern is with the lesser category that could be shared with the priest's household, unlike the most holy portions reserved for the priests in a holy place, Leviticus 6:16-18 and 6:26.

Verse 3 uses an unusual form of the cutting off formula: the unclean priest 'must be cut off from My presence,' literally 'from before Me,' rather than the more common 'from his people.' For a priest, whose whole life was lived before God, the sanction is framed as loss of the one thing that defined him.

Verse 9 says the priests 'must keep My charge,' shamar mishmeret, a phrase with a cognate object: literally 'guard My guarding.' It is the same phrase used when Aaron and his sons remained at the tent entrance seven days during their ordination 'and keep the LORD's charge so that you will not die,' Leviticus 8:35. Priests are guards of holy things.

The word 'outsider' in verses 10 and 13 is zar, a stranger or unauthorised person. The same word describes the 'unauthorized fire' of Nadab and Abihu, Leviticus 10:1, and the 'outsider who approaches the tabernacle' in Numbers 3:10. Zar does not mean foreigner by birth; a native Israelite who was not a priest was zar with respect to the holy food.

The standard for offerings is tamim, 'unblemished' or whole. The word reaches well beyond animals. Noah was 'blameless,' tamim, Genesis 6:9; God told Abraham, 'walk before Me and be blameless,' Genesis 17:1; and of God Himself it is said, 'His work is perfect,' Deuteronomy 32:4, and 'His way is perfect,' Psalm 18:30. The word describes integrity, completeness without flaw. Its opposite is mum, defect.

The aim of the offering is ratzon, 'acceptance' or favour. Verse 19 says literally 'for your acceptance,' as Leviticus 1:3 does. The word later names 'the year of the LORD's favor,' Isaiah 61:2, which Jesus read in the synagogue at Nazareth and declared fulfilled, Luke 4:19-21. The acceptance the unblemished animal secured for one worshipper becomes a year of favour proclaimed to all.

Finally, verse 32 says 'I must be acknowledged as holy,' using the passive reflexive stem of qadash, literally 'I will be sanctified.' The same form appears in Leviticus 10:3, 'I will show My holiness,' and in Ezekiel 36:23, where God promises to show the holiness of His great name. The Septuagint renders the verb with hagiazo, the verb of 'hallowed be Your name,' Matthew 6:9.

typology.type: The unblemished animal required for acceptance, verses 19-21
typology.fulfillment: Every burnt and peace offering had to be tamim, whole and without defect, to be accepted on the worshipper's behalf. The New Testament uses the Septuagint's word for this, amomos, of Christ: He 'offered Himself unblemished to God,' Hebrews 9:14, and believers are redeemed 'with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot,' 1 Peter 1:19. The escalation is that the animals were physically whole but could not take away sins, Hebrews 10:4. Christ is morally perfect, 'who knew no sin,' 2 Corinthians 5:21, and His one offering secures acceptance forever.

typology.type: The priestly household fed from the altar, including the slave bought with money, verses 10-11
typology.fulfillment: A guest or hired worker could not eat the holy food, but a slave purchased with the priest's own money or born in his house belonged to the family and ate. Paul's language for believers echoes this: 'you were bought at a price,' 1 Corinthians 6:20, and are 'no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household,' Ephesians 2:19. The escalation is that Christ's purchase makes not slaves but sons, Galatians 4:7, who eat at His table. Hebrews 13:10 says 'We have an altar' from which the old priests had no right to eat.

typology.type: Washing and waiting until evening before eating the holy food, verses 6-7
typology.fulfillment: An unclean priest had to bathe and wait for sunset before he could eat what was holy. The cleansing was real but temporary and had to be repeated every time. Hebrews invites believers to 'draw near with a sincere heart... having our hearts sprinkled to cleanse us from a guilty conscience and our bodies washed with pure water,' Hebrews 10:22. The type falls short because it cleansed the body for a day; Christ's blood cleanses the conscience, Hebrews 9:14, and the believer is washed once for all, 1 Corinthians 6:11, though still called to walk in the light, 1 John 1:7.

typology.type: The thank offering eaten the same day, verses 29-30
typology.fulfillment: The thanksgiving sacrifice had to be eaten on the day it was offered, nothing left until morning. It was a joyful, immediate meal of gratitude before God. Hebrews carries the thank offering into the church: 'Through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name,' Hebrews 13:15. The escalation is that the one day meal becomes continual praise, and the meal at the centre of Christian worship is the Lord's Supper, where believers give thanks for the body and blood of Christ, 1 Corinthians 11:24.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through its standard. Page after page, the worshipper is told that nothing with a defect will be accepted. The New Testament answers that God has found the one offering that meets the standard perfectly. Christ 'offered Himself unblemished to God,' Hebrews 9:14. Peter says believers were redeemed 'with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot,' 1 Peter 1:19, and he adds that Christ 'was known before the foundation of the world,' 1 Peter 1:20. The standard of Leviticus 22 was always pointing to a Lamb God Himself would provide.

It leads to Christ through acceptance. The recurring word of the chapter, ratzon, acceptance, answers the worshipper's deepest question: will God receive me? In Leviticus the answer depended on the animal. In the gospel it depends on Christ. Paul speaks of God's glorious grace 'which He has freely given us in the Beloved One,' Ephesians 1:6. The Father's word at Jesus' baptism, 'This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased,' Matthew 3:17, is the voice of acceptance that all who are in Him now share.

It leads to Christ through the priestly table. The chapter guards who may eat the holy food. Jesus says, 'Whoever eats My flesh and drinks My blood has eternal life,' John 6:54, and He gives His disciples bread and cup at the Last Supper. Believers are not guests or hired hands at that table but members of the household, bought with a price.

It leads to Christ through the hallowing of God's name. The chapter ends, 'I must be acknowledged as holy among the Israelites.' Jesus taught His disciples to pray, 'hallowed be Your name,' Matthew 6:9, and near the cross He prayed, 'Father, glorify Your name!' John 12:28. His obedience unto death was the supreme act of honouring the Father's name, which Israel's priests had so often profaned.

It leads to Christ through contrast with careless worship. Malachi's priests offered what cost them nothing. Christ offered what cost Him everything, 'He sacrificed for sin once for all when He offered up Himself,' Hebrews 7:27. The Priest and the Offering are one person.

These links are not imposed on the chapter. Hebrews and 1 Peter make them explicitly, using the chapter's own vocabulary of the unblemished offering.
study.god:
The chapter shows first that God's name is His honour and that He guards it. 'You must not profane My holy name,' He says at the beginning and end, verses 2 and 32. God is not indifferent to how He is treated. The name stands for His revealed character, the LORD who brought Israel out of Egypt, verse 33, and to handle His holy things carelessly is to say that His character does not matter. Ezekiel 36:22-23 shows the same God acting 'for My holy name' when His people had profaned it among the nations.

He is the God who deserves the best. The standard of tamim rejects the idea that God can be given leftovers. He is 'a great King,' Malachi 1:14, and His people's gifts reveal what they think of Him. Yet the chapter's God is not greedy. He allows a freewill offering with a stunted limb, verse 23, and He provides a way back from accidental sin by restitution, verse 14. His holiness is exacting but not arbitrary.

He is the God who shares His table. The holy food was God's, but He gave it to the priests and their households as their sustenance, verse 7, 'for they are his food.' Worship in Israel was not only giving to God; it was eating with Him. The same generosity shows in verse 13, where the widowed daughter returns to her father's table. God makes room in His household.

He is the God who cares for the life He has made. The rules of verses 27 and 28, keeping the newborn with its mother and not slaughtering both on one day, show a Creator who notices the bond between a cow and her calf. His holiness is not cold.

He is the God who sanctifies. 'I am the LORD who sanctifies you,' verse 32. Holiness is His gift before it is Israel's task. That holds together a real tension in the chapter: God demands a perfection His people cannot supply, and He supplies what He demands. The final answer is Christ, whom God set forth as the unblemished Lamb.

For worship, the chapter asks believers to give God their best and not their leftovers, to approach His table with self-examination, and to pray first of all that His name be hallowed.

crossReferences.note: Nadab and Abihu offered 'unauthorized fire' and died, and God said, 'To those who come near Me I will show My holiness.' Leviticus 22 turns the lesson into standing law. The word for unauthorised, zar, is the word for the 'outsider' who may not eat the holy food in 22:10.

The Passover law makes the same distinction as Leviticus 22:10-11: a purchased slave may eat after circumcision, but a temporary resident or hired hand may not. Belonging to the household, not mere presence in it, gives access to the holy meal.

God rebukes priests who offer blind, lame and sick animals and despise His name. The passage reads like Leviticus 22 turned into an indictment, and it adds the promise that God's name will be great among the nations, with pure offerings 'in every place.'

David refuses a free threshing floor and oxen: 'I will not offer to the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing.' He states as a principle what the unblemished standard of Leviticus 22:19-22 required in practice.

God says He will act for His holy name, which Israel profaned among the nations, and will show its holiness. Leviticus 22:32 warned, 'You must not profane My holy name.' Ezekiel shows God vindicating His name Himself when His people failed.

Christ 'offered Himself unblemished to God' to purify our consciences. The Greek word for unblemished is the Septuagint's term for the tamim animals of Leviticus 22. What the animal had physically, Christ had morally, and His offering reaches the conscience.

Believers were redeemed not with silver or gold but with 'the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot.' Peter uses the standard of Leviticus 22:19-21 to describe the one sacrifice that truly redeems.

Paul urges believers to offer their bodies 'as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God.' The acceptability Leviticus 22 required of an animal now describes the whole life of the believer, offered in response to God's mercy.

Paul calls his ministry 'priestly service of the gospel' so that the Gentiles might become 'an offering acceptable to God, sanctified by the Holy Spirit.' The language of Leviticus 22 is applied to people, and to nations once outside Israel's altar.

Believers are 'no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household.' Leviticus 22:10-11 excluded guests and hired hands from the holy food but included those who belonged to the household. In Christ, outsiders become household members.

The priest of Leviticus 22:6 had to bathe and wait for sunset before he could eat the holy things, and do it again after every defilement. Hebrews applies that washing to the conscience: those cleansed by Christ's blood are invited to come near to God now, in full assurance.

Whoever eats the Lord's Supper 'in an unworthy manner' is guilty, so each must examine himself first. The warning echoes Leviticus 22:3 and 22:9, where careless eating of holy food brought guilt and death.

Jesus teaches His disciples to pray first, 'hallowed be Your name.' Leviticus 22:32 says, 'I must be acknowledged as holy among the Israelites.' The closing concern of the holiness laws becomes the opening petition of Christian prayer.

study.oneStory:
The story of offerings begins outside Eden. Cain and Abel both brought gifts, and 'the LORD looked with favor on Abel and his offering, but He had no regard for Cain and his offering,' Genesis 4:4-5. From the first, the Bible raises the question this chapter answers: what makes an offering acceptable to God? Abel brought 'the best portions of the firstborn of his flock.' The best was given, and it was received.

At Sinai the question was answered in detail. Leviticus 22 fixes the standard: whole, unblemished, costly, brought by clean hands and eaten by the household that belongs to God. It gives Israel a way to be accepted, and it guards God's name from contempt. But the standard also exposes the problem. Priests grew careless, worshippers cheated, and by Malachi's day God said He would rather someone shut the temple doors, Malachi 1:10. Even when the animals were perfect, they could not remove sin, Hebrews 10:4.

The story turns when God provides the offering Himself. Abraham had told Isaac, 'God Himself will provide the lamb,' Genesis 22:8. John the Baptist points to Jesus: 'Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!' John 1:29. He is without blemish, offered once, accepted by the Father, and raised as the proof of that acceptance. Through Him God's name is hallowed, and outsiders become members of God's household who eat at His table.

The church now offers what Leviticus pictured: bodies as living sacrifices, praise from the lips, generosity to others, Hebrews 13:15-16, all made acceptable through Christ.

The story ends in the new creation, where God's people are presented 'holy and blameless,' Ephesians 5:27, and where the Lamb is at the centre of the throne, Revelation 7:17. Nothing unclean will enter, Revelation 21:27, not because the standard has been lowered but because the Lamb has made His people whole. The holy name will be on their foreheads, and they will serve Him forever.

quiz.q: What was required of a priest before he could eat the sacred offerings, if he had become ceremonially unclean?

options.text: He had to bathe with water and wait until evening before eating.
options.note: Verses 6-7 specify this exact requirement.

options.text: He was permanently barred from eating the sacred food.
options.note: Verses 6-7 describe a temporary, not permanent, restriction resolved by washing and time.

options.text: No restriction applied to unclean priests.
options.note: Verses 4-6 explicitly restrict an unclean priest from eating the sacred food until clean.

options.text: He had to offer an additional sacrifice before eating.
options.note: The text specifies washing and waiting until evening, not an additional sacrifice.

quiz.q: Who, besides the priest himself, was permitted to eat the sacred offerings within a priestly household?

options.text: Members of his household, including a slave bought with his money or born in his house, and an unmarried or widowed daughter who had returned home.
options.note: Verses 10-13 detail exactly these permitted members.

options.text: Any hired worker or guest visiting the priest's home.
options.note: Verse 10 explicitly excludes a hired hand or guest from eating the sacred offerings.

options.text: Any Israelite who happened to be nearby.
options.note: Verse 10 restricts this specifically to the priest's own household, not the general public.

options.text: No one besides the priest himself could ever eat it.
options.note: Verses 11-13 explicitly extend this privilege to certain household members.

quiz.q: What standard did every animal offered to the LORD have to meet, according to verses 19-25?

options.text: It had to be without blemish or defect.
options.note: Verses 19-25 repeat and detail this requirement extensively.

options.text: It had to be the largest animal available.
options.note: The text specifies flawlessness, not size, as the required standard.

options.text: Any animal was acceptable regardless of condition.
options.note: Verses 20 and 22 explicitly reject animals with defects.

options.text: No standard is given for sacrificial animals in this chapter.
options.note: Verses 19-25 give this standard in explicit detail.

quiz.q: How old did an ox, sheep, or goat have to be before it could be offered as a sacrifice, according to verse 27?

options.text: At least eight days old, having remained with its mother for the first seven days.
options.note: Verse 27 states this requirement directly.

options.text: At least one full year old.
options.note: The text specifies eight days as the minimum, not a full year, for this particular requirement.

options.text: No minimum age is specified.
options.note: Verse 27 explicitly gives an eight day minimum.

options.text: It must be newborn, offered on its very first day.
options.note: Verse 27 explicitly requires it remain with its mother for seven days first.

quiz.q: How does 1 Peter 1:18-19 connect to this chapter's standard for sacrificial animals?

options.text: It describes Christ as a lamb without blemish or defect, whose blood redeems believers.
options.note: 1 Peter 1:18-19 uses language that directly echoes this chapter's required standard.

options.text: It rejects the idea that any sacrifice needs to be without blemish.
options.note: 1 Peter 1:19 affirms, rather than rejects, this very standard by applying it to Christ.

options.text: It has no relationship to Old Testament sacrificial standards.
options.note: 1 Peter 1:19 draws directly on this Old Testament vocabulary and standard.

options.text: It applies this standard only to Old Testament animals, never to Christ.
options.note: 1 Peter 1:19 explicitly applies this standard to Christ Himself.

questions: This chapter insists that God's people not treat holy things carelessly. Where in your own life, worship, giving, service, has familiarity bred a kind of casualness that God's holiness deserves better than?
Only an unblemished animal was acceptable, however sincerely offered. Where might you be tempted to offer God your leftovers, time, energy, attention, rather than your best?

Priests had to wait and wash before approaching the sacred offerings again after becoming unclean. What ordinary, patient practices help you return to close fellowship with God after a season of distance or failure?

Christ is the spotless Lamb who met the standard this chapter could only demand, never produce. How does resting in His sufficiency, rather than your own performance, change the way you approach God today?
God cared deeply that His name not be profaned by careless worship among His people. Where do your public words or actions, at church, at work, online, risk misrepresenting God's character to others?

translationNotes.note: Bear the guilt and die reflects the seriousness with which careless priestly handling of sacred things was regarded, treating negligence in worship as a capital, not merely ceremonial, matter.
Add a fifth to its value describes the restitution required for eating a sacred offering by mistake, the same proportion required elsewhere in Leviticus for guilt offerings involving property.

The prohibition on slaughtering a mother and her young on the same day likely reflects a broader biblical concern for mercy even within permitted practices, echoed in Deuteronomy's law against taking a mother bird with her young.
